implementation_notes: The mainstream Java form today: annotate the coarse class @Service, inject the fine-grained collaborators through the constructor, and put the unit of work on the facade method with @Transactional - Spring's AOP proxy replaces the EJB container's container-managed transaction and supplies propagation, isolation and rollback rules declaratively. Keep the contract coarse, because the transaction should mark the workflow entry, not the individual repository calls; the classic form is still justified (a plain class instead of transaction scripts) exactly here, since the boundary must be a named, proxied bean method. Choose this variant when the application runs on Spring Boot 3+ (Java 17 floor) and does not need Jakarta EE portability.
pitfalls: @Transactional on a self-invoked method is a no-op (the proxy is bypassed): the coarse entry must be the call arriving from outside the bean, not an internal this.call().
Rollback happens for unchecked exceptions only by default; checked exceptions need rollbackFor or the workflow commits partial work.
Doing HTTP/gRPC calls inside the transactional method holds a database connection for the duration; keep remote work outside the boundary.

variants.name: Stateless session bean facade (classic J2EE)
variants.idiom_name: @Stateless session bean exposing a coarse business interface
variants.implementation_notes: The pattern's namesake realization: an @Stateless session bean (or @Stateful for a genuine multi-step conversation) whose business interface - or no-interface view for local callers - exposes one coarse method per use case; the Enterprise Bean container pools stateless instances, demarcates one container-managed transaction per business method by default, rolls back on unchecked exceptions, and applies declarative security, so the facade code itself contains no transaction API calls. Design the business interface as the boundary and keep it coarse, because remote business interfaces serialize every parameter and returning entity beans across them is both slow and a coupling trap. Choose this variant on a Jakarta EE container, or when a stateful, container-managed conversation object is required.
pitfalls: A @Stateful facade scales with conversations, not requests: it must be removed explicitly (@Remove) or the container accumulates passivated instances until timeout.
A remote business interface serializes every parameter and return value; coarse Transfer Objects are mandatory there, and exposing entity beans over it leaks the model.
Pooled stateless beans must hold no per-request state in instance fields - the instance serving the next call is not the one that served the previous request.
